t: Verbal Arithmetic Puzzle — Column-Wise Backtracking with Carry
o: We must assign a distinct digit 0–9 to each distinct uppercase letter so that decoding every word as a number (no leading zeros) makes the sum of the left-side words equal the decoded result. In Example 1, mapping S→9, E→5, N→6, D→7, M→1, O→0, R→8, Y→2 gives 9567 + 1085 = 10652, so the answer is true. Example 2 works similarly with three addends, while Example 3 has no valid assignment because the required digit collisions would occur. The constraints are tiny: at most 10 distinct characters, at most 7 characters per word, and at most 5 words. This means an exhaustive search over assignments is feasible, but naive enumeration of all $10!$ permutations can be wasteful; pruning by processing the equation column by column (like hand addition, right to left, carrying between columns) cuts the search dramatically.
k: There are at most 10 distinct letters, so a full assignment search space is at most 10! ≈ 3.6M — small enough to brute force with pruning.
Adding numbers by hand works column by column from the right with a carry; simulating this lets us prune invalid partial mappings long before all letters are assigned.
Leading-zero constraints only apply to the first character of each word and of the result, so those letters simply cannot be assigned digit 0.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Digit Permutations
a.i: Collect the distinct letters, try every way of assigning them distinct digits from 0–9, and for each complete assignment verify no leading zero exists and that the decoded sum matches. With ≤10 letters there are at most $P(10,10)=10!$ assignments, which is fast enough given the tiny input sizes. This is the most direct translation of the problem statement into code.
s: Collect all distinct characters into a list; if more than 10, return false immediately.
Recursively assign unused digits 0–9 to each character in order, marking digits as used.
When all characters are assigned, check that the first character of every word and of the result is not 0.
Decode each word to its numeric value and compare the sum of the words against the decoded result.
Return true if any assignment satisfies the equation, otherwise false after exhausting all.
a.t: O(P(10,k) · L) where k ≤ 10 is the number of distinct letters and L is the total string length — up to 10! complete assignments, each verified in linear time.
a.sp: O(k) for the recursion stack, mapping, and used-digit array.

a.i: Simulate grade-school addition: process columns from rightmost to leftmost, summing the digits of the words in the current column plus the incoming carry. When the column ends, the resulting digit must match the corresponding result character and the outgoing carry passes to the next column. Letters encountered without an assignment get one on the spot, skipping digits already taken and digit 0 for leading characters. This prunes huge portions of the search space early — most wrong prefixes die within the first couple of columns instead of after a full assignment.
s: If any word is longer than the result, return false (the sum cannot be that short).
Build the column structure: for offset i from 0 upward, collect the characters appearing at position len(word)-1-i across all words.
Recurse over (column, row, running column sum, carry). If the current letter is unmapped, try each free digit (skipping 0 for leading letters), assign, and recurse.
At the end of a column, compute total = sum + carry; the result character at this column must equal total % 10 (assigning it if needed), and the recursion continues with carry = total / 10.
Success is reaching past the last column with carry 0; backtrack (unassign) whenever a branch fails.
a.t: O(10^k · k) worst case in theory, but in practice far less due to per-column pruning via the carry constraint; with k ≤ 10 letters and ≤ 7 columns this runs in milliseconds.
a.sp: O(k + C) for the mapping, used array, recursion depth, and column storage, where C is the result length.

w: In an interview, start by stating the brute-force bound (at most 10! assignments) to show the problem is tractable, then present the column-wise backtracking solution as the polished answer — it demonstrates both insight (mirroring manual addition) and engineering (pruning). Common pitfalls: forgetting the no-leading-zero rule for **every** word and the result (not just the result), allowing two letters to share a digit, mishandling words shorter than the result (they contribute nothing to high columns), and missing the final check that the carry must be exactly 0 after the last column. Edge cases worth testing: single-letter words, a result only one digit longer than the longest word, and repeated letters within a word. Likely follow-ups: count the number of valid solutions instead of returning one, generalize to subtraction or multiplication cryptarithms, or handle inputs with more than 10 distinct characters (answer would always be false under the distinctness rule).
